content.title: Layers of Inequality in Energy Access
content.intro: M2: Energy Access and Inclusive Energy Services

content.text: Lesson 2 Overview

As explained earlier in this module, electricity access is a critical driver of sustainable development, yet vast disparities persist worldwide.

This section explores recent data on global electricity access, revealing both significant progress and ongoing challenges across different regions, urban and rural areas, and specific vulnerable contexts.


Through a comprehensive analysis of energy access disparities, we can identify the underlying factors driving energy inequality - required developing targeted strategies to narrow the gap and ensure equitable access for all.

concepts.body: Access to clean cooking refers to the availability and use of safe, efficient, and environmentally friendly cooking methods and fuels, which reduce health risks and environmental impact compared to traditional cooking practices.

concepts.title: heating and cooling fuels and technologies
concepts.body: Heating and cooling fuels and technologies refer to the various energy sources (like natural gas, electricity, and renewable options) and systems (such as furnaces, heat pumps, and air conditioners) used to regulate indoor temperatures for comfort and efficiency.

content.text: Progress has been made in recent decades, with global electricity access rising from 78% in 2000 to 92% in 2023. However, a different picture emerges when breaking down electricity access along global energy access gap - i.e., by country type, urban vs. rural areas, and considering additional layers, as described to follow.
The Tracking SDG7: The Energy Progress Report 2025 presents a comprehensive landscape of energy access progress and deficits.

content.intro: M2: Energy Access and Inclusive Energy Services
content.title: A: The Urban - Rural Divide

content.text:
The energy divide is particularly significant between urban and rural areas around the world. While urban centers generally benefit from established infrastructure, many rural communities remain underserved.



This section explores the urban - rural energy access gap. We will examine the primary factors driving these inequalities and discuss current trends and key element to consider to promote universal access to sustainable energy.
Electricity Access in Rural Areas

content.body: In 2023, urban areas globally achieved an impressive 98 percent electrification rate.

Annually, an average of 73.1 million people gained electricity access between 2021 and 2023, outpacing population growth. This remarkable trend was particularly prominent in Central Asia which significantly narrowed its access gap.
Informal peri-urban settlements pose substantial challenges to achieving 100 percent urban electrification.

content.text: The lack of electricity infrastructure in rural areas hampers not only domestic activities but also limits opportunities for education, healthcare, and economic development.
Last Mile and Isolated rural populations

Last-mile communities are the hardest-to-reach populations and face mounting challenges in accessing energy.

Typically located in remote, low-density rural areas, extending traditional grids to these regions is economically unfeasible and logistically complex. These remote communities usually depend on minimal or subsistence economic activity, face physical barriers to accessibility, and are considerably distant from external markets. In this context, infrastructure costs are high, and limited access to financial resources restricts the adoption of off-grid solutions.

Mountain areas, where 1.05 billion people lived in 2015 (14% of the global population), are a prominent example. Population density decreases with altitude, and communities at higher elevations experience harsher weather, heightening energy needs for cooking, space heating, and water heating.

Protected areas are rapidly expanding and projected to cover 30% of land and sea by 2030. (Mouillot et al., 2024). These territories may face more restrictive regulations, which can limit infrastructure development and pose regulatory barriers to electrification projects.

In some regions, migration to urban areas has reshaped local demographics making these remote communities more vulnerable. Trends include the “feminization” of agriculture, where men migrate for work while women maintain rural livelihoods (CGIAR, 2021).
Example

In Koh Kantheay, Cambodia, UNDP supported a microgrid project to provide isolated communities with reliable energy access. This model, based on public-private-community partnerships, included a 70% public subsidy for initial infrastructure setup and a 30% contribution from private energy entrepreneurs, who oversee grid operations. This project demonstrates the potential of solar microgrids to deliver sustainable energy access to remote communities, fostering public-private partnerships 💬️ and reducing investment risk (UNDP Cambodia, 2023).

Developing sustainable off-grid energy solutions in last-mile areas , like solar microgrid, presented in the case study above, demands tailored technical support and long-term financing mechanisms. These instruments will be presented in more details in the following modules.

content.text: Electricity Access in Urban Areas

Urbanization rates are accelerating worldwide, further stressing energy access in cities.

With the global population reaching 8 billion in November 2022, more than half (55%) now live in urban areas—a number projected to rise to 70% by 2050. Much of this urban growth occurs in small cities and intermediate towns, compounding existing inequalities and urban poverty (UNSTATS, 2023).

As cities expand, so does their energy consumption. Urban areas consume two-thirds of the world's energy (UNEP, 2021), demanding an uninterrupted supply to meet the needs of residents.

Rapid urbanization, aging electricity grids, and unplanned expansions can lead to inefficiencies, blackouts, and higher costs.

Additionally, socioeconomic inequalities mean that modern energy services are often unaffordable for the most vulnerable populations.

Greater efforts are needed to ensure that all urban residents benefit from sustainable and inclusive energy solutions.
The Energy Progress Report provides critical insights into urban electrification as of 2023:

content.body: In 2023, urban areas globally achieved an impressive 97.8 percent electrification rate.

Annually, an average of 73.1 million people gained electricity access between 2021 and 2023, outpacing population growth. This remarkable trend was particularly prominent in Central and Southern Asia.
Informal peri-urban settlements pose substantial challenges to achieving 100 percent urban electrification.

content.text:
The prevalence of modern energy solutions in urban settings contributes to improved living standards, facilitates economic activities, and supports the overall dynamism of urban life.
However, there are important exceptions - as outlined in the next section on informal settlements.

content.title: B: Informal Settlements and Underserved Neighborhoods

content.text: 1.1 billion people live in informal settlements worldwide.

Informal settlements or slums (ISs) are typically defined as densely populated areas characterized by inadequate housing and limited access to essential services such as clean water, sanitation, and electricity. Although these challenges are not exclusive to ISs, they are more prevalent and acute in such settings. The lack of formal infrastructure in ISs often results in heightened vulnerability to hazards, limited mobility, poor waste management, and exposure to health and safety risks, making these issues not only more common but also more critical than in other urban areas.

These neighborhoods often emerge without formal planning and lack legal recognition, which exacerbates the challenges residents face regarding infrastructure, health, and economic opportunities.

Over 1.1 billion people live in ISs globally (WEF, 2023) and rapid urbanization projects that number could double in the next 30 years, particularly in developing regions (Kuffer et. al., 2019). In Sub-Saharan Africa, more than half of the urban population lives currently lives in in ISs.

The following figure illustrates the many forms that energy access can take in ISs - both formal or informal, with payments to landlords, the utility or electricity reseller, and diverse connection types. Many such connection types - such as as direct line tapping (Type C), meter bypasses (Type D), and using extension cords strung precariously (Type E) pose immediate safety hazards

Understanding the economic realities that push residents towards informal connections, along with the social dynamics within these communities, is crucial to improving energy access in ISs. Governments, the private sector, and communities can all take steps toward improving this access.

The starting point is recognizing informal settlements as a symptom of social inequality, not a crime. Historically, enforcement actions have bred distrust between utilities and ISs, hindering cooperation. Collaboration is key to improving services. Utilities must shift from punishment to partnership, engaging the informal electricity market to create a win-win situation.

Legal recognition of ISs is also essential to formalize access to safer, regulated electricity.

content.title: C: Small Island Developing States (SIDS)

content.text:
small island developing states 💬️ (SIDS) are a group of 57 island nations with a combined population of approximately 65 million.

Due to their remote geographical locations, these populations face distinct social, economic, and environmental challenges along with unique energy access difficulties.

As of 2021, the average electricity access rate in SIDS was around 91%, and access to clean cooking stood at 58%, significantly below the global average of 74% (UNDP., 2025). These averages, however, mask important disparities between and within countries.

Geographic isolation, small markets, and reliance on imported fossil fuels make energy in SIDS expensive and volatile. Fossil fuels still make up around 75% of the electricity mix in SIDS, with approximately 60% of them importing over 90% of their fossil fuel needs . This leads to high energy costs, up to four times higher than in continental regions, with frequent supply disruptions and high public subsidies. For instance, fossil fuel subsidies reached 8% of GDP in Suriname and 3.7% in Timor-Leste, severely straining public finances that could be directed toward clean energy investments.

While some SIDS like Singapore, Barbados, and the Maldives have achieved near-universal access, others face major deficits. In Papua New Guinea, only 19% of the population had access to electricity in 2022., while Vanuatu’s electricity access rate stood at 70%, and 37.4% in Guinea-Bissau. The rural-urban divide is stark, with only 1.2% of rural residents having electricity access in Haiti compared to 79.9% in urban areas, while in Kiribati rural clean cooking access is 2% versus 20% in urban areas.

A crucial consideration in providing energy access to small islands and their communities is the diversity of cultures and languages, which influences demand profiles and livelihoods. Understanding these nuances is essential for designing decentralized renewable energy projects tailored to specific community needs.

Example:
In the Solomon Islands, where 24% of the population lacks electricity, the heavy reliance on imported oil results in high energy costs. To address this, the country has invested in off-grid solar PV systems, transforming over 100 households by providing access to sustainable energy, thereby improving education, livelihoods, and resilience (UNDP, 2023).

content.title: D: Fragile and Conflict Contexts

content.text: Refugee Camps and Forcibly Displaced Populations

At mid-2024, the number of people forced to flee conflict, violence, human rights violations, and persecution exceeded 122 million (UNHCR, 2024).
More than 6.6 million people live in refugee camps and more than 94% of households in camps lack access to electricity, while while 81% rely on firewood or charcoal for cooking. This reliance exacerbates environmental degradation, increases health risks, and impacts the safety of vulnerable populations, particularly women and children.

Refugee camps are frequently located in remote areas, where limited infrastructure and high logistics costs further complicate the provision of energy. To address this, humanitarian agencies spend over $108 million annually on diesel fuel, resulting in over 194,000 tons of CO₂ emissions (UNEP, 2023) (UN Refugees, 2021)

Refugee camps face acute energy needs due to dense populations and limited infrastructure. Decentralized renewable energy systems, such as solar mini-grids, are emerging as effective alternatives. These systems are faster to deploy and less capital-intensive than centralized grids, making them more adaptable to remote and temporary camp settings.

While humanitarian aid provides temporary energy solutions, studies have calculated that cost savings could be possible by providing distributed energy systems to camps that might be established for years and not months (Lehne et al., 2016). This context requires a transition to scalable, resilient energy options that can be managed and maintained locally over time.

Example
In the UNDP-supported camp in Salahley, Hargeisa, Somalia, small investments in solar infrastructure have brought significant improvements. solar energy 💬️ now powers essential services for over 600 internally displaced families, providing a safe and reliable energy lifeline in a remote village 50 kilometers outside Hargeisa.
Environmental hazards, crisis and conflict settings

Major crises across the globe, spanning from Afghanistan to Congo, Haiti, Palestine, Ukraine, Sudan, Yemen, and beyond, have inflicted significant, sometimes generational setbacks to development progress, leaving people in these contexts facing an increasingly uncertain future.


Approximately 15 percent of the world’s total population – roughly 1.2 billion people – reside in conflict-affected areas (UNDP, 2022), while disaster losses have sharply risen, impacting 4.2 billion individuals over the past two decades (UNDRR, 2020).


Example: The impact of energy loss is starkly illustrated by nighttime images of areas hit by disasters or conflict, such as power outages following Cyclone Fani or widespread blackouts during the Ukraine war, showing the devastating impact of disrupted energy access in these fragile settings.

image.caption: Lights Out before and after Ukraine war (Earth Observation, 2022)

content.text:
Resilient energy infrastructure plays a crucial role in post-crisis recovery.

the undp sustainable energy hub 💬️ (SEH) defines energy resilience in fragile contexts as the ability of individuals, communities, and systems to withstand and recover from shocks and stresses related to energy supply, demand, and access. For instance, recovery plans can include tailored strategies for sustainable and resilient energy integration, such as financing mechanisms to de-risk investments and incentivize private sector participation to address funding shortages.

The intersection of the climate crisis and fragility underscores the need for long-term resilience planning. For example, integrating renewable energy into health systems during crises, as demonstrated in past outbreaks like COVID-19, has shown that sustainable energy can simultaneously address immediate needs and create pathways for green recovery.

Energy access in fragile and conflict contexts requires targeted interventions that combine immediate solutions with long-term sustainable strategies. Decentralized renewable energy systems—such as solar home systems, mini-grids, solar-powered water pumps, and portable clean energy units—offer adaptable and rapidly deployable solutions that can operate independently of vulnerable central grids.

These systems can be well-suited for remote or insecure areas where infrastructure is damaged or non-existent. By scaling such technologies, fostering innovative financing mechanisms, and embedding energy resilience into broader recovery and development strategies, it is possible to mitigate the impacts of crises and ensure more reliable support for vulnerable populations.
Least Developed Countries (LDCs) and regions impacted by fragility, conflict, and violence (FCV)

Least Developed Countries (LDCs) and regions impacted by fragility, conflict, and violence (FCV) face additional challenges. Between 2020 and 2023, energy access gains slowed in these areas, leaving approximately 476 million people in LDCs and over 427 million in FCV countries without electricity.
Access to electricity in community services and public institutions

Nearly 1 billion people in low- and lower-middle-income countries rely on health-care facilities with unreliable or no electricity. In South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, 12% and 15% of health-care facilities lack electricity access, with only half of hospitals in sub-Saharan Africa having reliable power, especially in rural areas. (WHO, 2023)

In addition, globally, 77.4% of primary schools and 90.6% of upper secondary schools have electricity access. In sub-Saharan Africa, only 32% of primary and 52.2% of upper secondary schools are electrified, while in least developed countries, access rates are 38% and 60.4%, respectively (Our World in Data, 2022).
Technologies status and trends

Decentralized renewable energy offers a viable solution to electrify hard-to-reach rural areas, home to many of the remaining unconnected populations. In 2022, the IEA reported that solar home and lighting systems brought electricity to 2.5 million households, with off-grid solar solutions serving an estimated 490 million people. Of these, 158 million had solar access meeting international quality standards. Additionally, 47 million people were connected to 19,000 mini-grids, with hydropower and solar accounting for one-third of these installations (IEA et al., 2024).

million people were serviced
through off-grid solar solutions in 2022.

These variations in electricity access highlight the vast differences in how countries and institutions define and measure access. In some contexts, electricity access is defined simply as a physical connection to the grid, regardless of quality or reliability. In others, it includes minimum service levels such as the ability to power basic appliances, number of hours of supply per day, or affordability.

For example, India considers a village electrified if at least 10% of households and public institutions have access to electricity (PRS India., 2017) while the World Bank’s Multi-Tier Framework (MTF) assesses access based on capacity, duration, reliability, quality, affordability, legality, and safety (ESMAP, 2015). These contrasting definitions can lead to major discrepancies in reporting and in understanding the real impact of electrification efforts.

To ensure meaningful progress toward universal energy access, strategies must be tailored to regional and national contexts, taking into account not just connection rates but also the quality, reliability, and inclusiveness of energy services. This is particularly critical in underserved rural areas and informal settlements, where basic energy needs often remain unmet despite being counted as “electrified.”

takeaways.title: Energy access gaps run deeper than national averages.
takeaways.description: While global electrification rates have improved, millions remain underserved—especially in rural areas, informal settlements, and fragile contexts. Looking beyond national statistics reveals deep inequalities in the quality, reliability, and affordability of electricity access.

takeaways.title: Rural and last-mile communities face unique and persistent barriers.
takeaways.description: Remote, low-density areas often lack grid infrastructure and financing, making electrification costly and complex. Tailored off-grid solutions, such as solar microgrids, are essential to closing these gaps and ensuring equitable energy access.

takeaways.title: Urbanization brings both energy access opportunity and risk of deepening inequalities
takeaways.description: Urban areas generally have high electricity coverage, but rapid growth and informal expansion often leave low-income residents behind. Targeted investments in informal settlements and better urban energy planning are critical to delivering truly inclusive access.
